title: Velcro and the burr
hook: A walk with a dog, a coat full of burrs and a very patient Swiss engineer.
peek: After a walk in the Swiss countryside, an engineer found burrs clinging to his trousers and his dog's fur. Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks, and spent years turning the trick into a fastener.
lede: In the 1940s, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral came home from a walk to find burdock burrs stuck all over his trousers and his dog's coat. He looked at one under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks catching on loops of fabric and fur. It took him years of trial and error to copy that in a material that could be made by the mile.

bullets.text: Each burr is a seed head covered in stiff spines with hooked tips. The plant uses them to hitch rides on passing animals, which is exactly what happened to de Mestral's dog.
Cotton wore out too quickly. Nylon, sewn into loops and then cut, held its hooked shape, and de Mestral received a Swiss patent in 1955.
The name joins the French words for velvet and hook. De Mestral built a company around it, and early sales were slow until clothing and sports gear makers caught on.
Apollo crews used it to keep pens, food packets and tools from floating away inside the cabin, which helped make the fastener famous.
Velcro is a trademark, and in 2017 the company released a jokey music video asking people to say 'hook and loop' instead, to stop the brand name becoming an ordinary word.
